content: The World Health Organization (WHO) provides a structured, tiered approach to HIV patient monitoring, which is essential for effective clinical management and program evaluation. This system is designed to ensure the quality and continuity of HIV care and treatment for adults, pregnant and breastfeeding women, infants, and children. It generates data that allows programs to monitor patient health and treatment outcomes over time, as well as measure program performance across various healthcare facilities and geographic regions. HIV patient monitoring systems are integral components of broader health information systems, contributing to the delivery of HIV, maternal and child health (MNCH)/HIV, and tuberculosis (TB)/HIV services. These systems also enable the measurement of standardized indicators at subnational and national levels for both in-country and global reporting. Data routinely collected through patient monitoring in healthcare facilities can also serve as a critical source for case surveillance. The WHO emphasizes the importance of country-specific situation analyses to improve HIV case surveillance, patient monitoring, and the use of unique identifiers. These analyses should identify and cost incremental improvements. WHO provides tools to assist countries in conducting these analyses. The primary purpose of an HIV patient monitoring system is twofold: to enable effective clinical management of patients and to generate data for program monitoring. This system supports the monitoring of key clinical and programmatic indicators, optimizing HIV treatment linkages, retention, and outcomes over the medium term (5–15 years). It also facilitates reporting on subnational, national, and global indicators, providing critical information for decision-making and improving program and patient outcomes. The updated WHO guidance supports the capture of essential elements of clinical management and the HIV care cascade, including enrollment in care, retention, antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation, and viral suppression. It introduces a standardized, simplified, and integrated approach to patient monitoring, aiming to optimize outcomes for people living with HIV receiving ART over an extended period. One significant change in the updated guidance is the removal of the pre-ART register, as all confirmed HIV-positive individuals are now eligible for treatment. This shift aligns with the treat all approach, which eliminates the need for assessing ART eligibility and emphasizes early initiation of ART in all populations. The guidance also includes recommendations for transitioning from paper-based to electronic systems to improve monitoring and reporting. The minimum dataset for HIV patient monitoring includes a core set of demographic, clinical, and laboratory data elements with standardized definitions and coding categories. This dataset provides a comprehensive assessment of all individuals enrolled in HIV care and supports the standardization of patient information. It enables program staff to compare data across populations, time, and geographic areas, while also providing clinical teams with longitudinal data to monitor the quality of care along the HIV service cascade. The updated guidance incorporates new WHO recommendations on antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) for treatment and prevention, revised ART regimens, and updated approaches to infant prophylaxis. It also addresses the use of routine viral load monitoring to diagnose and confirm treatment failure, replacing the use of CD4 counts for follow-up. Additionally, it includes updates on managing co-infections and comorbidities, such as TB, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), and viral hepatitis, as well as the concept of differentiated care to improve service delivery. The guidance highlights the importance of integrating HIV patient monitoring with monitoring systems for related conditions, such as TB and NCDs, and across service delivery points, including maternal and child health (MNCH) and TB settings. It also emphasizes the need for harmonizing systems across program areas and within broader health management information systems (HMIS), whether paper-based or electronic, to ensure effective linkage and integration. At the facility level, healthcare providers and supervisors can use this guidance to identify key data elements and indicators for effective clinical care and program management, improve patient monitoring and retention, and enhance the quality of care. At subnational and national levels, program managers can use the guidance to analyze and utilize data, provide feedback to healthcare facility staff, and improve linkages, retention, and outcomes along the HIV care cascade. The guidance also includes a description of generic patient monitoring tools, such as the HIV patient card, ART register, and community-based monitoring tools, along with examples of these tools. It discusses special considerations for integrating and linking patient monitoring systems with TB, MNCH, and key population services, as well as monitoring early warning indicators (EWIs) for HIV drug resistance. Overall, the updated WHO guidance aims to support national HIV programs in managing, monitoring, and retaining an increasing number of people living with HIV on ART, while optimizing program and patient outcomes through a standardized and integrated approach to patient monitoring.
